lesson.title: Effective Collisions: Energy and Orientation Together
lesson.summary: Combines the energy and orientation requirements from collision theory into the single, precise definition of an effective collision, and quantifies how rarely both are satisfied at once.
lesson.body:
This final section of the unit ties together the two threads collision theory opened up. Collision theory established that a reaction requires particles to physically collide. Activation energy, the activated complex, and the transition state then established what has to happen, both energetically and structurally, at the instant of collision for a reaction to actually occur. An effective collision, then, is simply a collision that satisfies both requirements at the same time: sufficient kinetic energy, at least Ea, directed along the line connecting the colliding particles, and correct orientation, meaning the reactive parts of each particle are actually facing one another at the moment of impact.

Both conditions are necessary, and neither alone is sufficient, which is worth spelling out concretely. Two molecules could collide with far more than enough energy to react, yet still bounce apart completely unreacted if they happen to strike at the wrong angle, exposing the wrong atoms, or the wrong face of a larger molecule, to each other. Conversely, two molecules oriented perfectly for reaction will still simply bounce apart if they are moving too slowly, without enough combined energy to reach the transition state described in the previous two sections. Both filters have to be passed simultaneously, on the very same collision, for a reaction to actually happen.

Worked example, decomposing the headline number from the collision theory section into its two separate causes. Using the same illustrative total collision frequency introduced there, Z = 1.0 x 10^30 collisions per liter per second, suppose that only a fraction f = 1.0 x 10^-9 of those collisions bring enough combined kinetic energy to clear the activation energy barrier, and that of those sufficiently energetic collisions, only a fraction p = 1.0 x 10^-2, that is, 1 percent, happen to occur with the correct orientation. The overall effective collision rate is the product of all three factors together:

effective rate = Z x f x p = (1.0 x 10^30)(1.0 x 10^-9)(1.0 x 10^-2) = 1.0 x 10^19 collisions per liter per second

This lands exactly on the 1.0 x 10^19 effective collision rate introduced in the collision theory section. The combined fraction also checks out: f x p = (1.0 x 10^-9)(1.0 x 10^-2) = 1.0 x 10^-11, reproducing the "one collision in one hundred billion" figure computed there as well. Splitting that single overall fraction into an energy factor and a separate orientation factor is exactly what collision theory does for you: it explains why the success rate is so small by attributing it to two independent, physically distinct requirements, rather than leaving it as one mysterious, unexplained number.

It is worth being clear that the specific values used above, f = 1.0 x 10^-9 and p = 1.0 x 10^-2, are illustrative, chosen to demonstrate the relationship cleanly, not measured data for any one specific named reaction. Every real reaction has its own characteristic energy fraction and orientation factor, shaped by its own activation energy and by the size, shape, and complexity of the molecules involved. That is ultimately why different reactions proceed at such wildly different rates even when compared at the same temperature and the same concentration: some clear both filters, energy and orientation, quite easily, while others almost never do, and the entire kinetics unit, from the integrated rate laws at the start through collision theory here at the end, is the set of tools chemists use to describe and predict exactly how that plays out.
